claims.text: A chemically uniform precursor facilitates synchronized reduction of all alloying metal ions.
A chemically uniform precursor facilitates co-nucleation of all alloying metals.
Synchronized reduction and co-nucleation produce homogeneous high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
A mechanically blended precursor causes spatially heterogeneous reduction.
Spatially heterogeneous reduction leads to phase separation and elemental clustering.
A mixed-metal coordination compound can ensure molecular-scale uniformity of Au, Pd, Pt, Rh, and Ir precursors.
Spectroscopy can verify the molecular-scale uniformity of the mixed-metal precursor.
Keeping solvent, reducing agent, temperature, and hold time identical isolates precursor mixing state as the controlled difference.
Molecularly even metal-ion dispersion promotes simultaneous reduction and localized co-nucleation.
Non-uniform precursor distribution produces asynchronous reduction and localized nucleation.
The chemically homogeneous precursor will yield a single-phase nanoparticle structure.
The chemically homogeneous precursor will yield uniformly distributed Au, Pd, Pt, Rh, and Ir.
The chemically homogeneous precursor will yield nanoparticles with high exposure of catalytic surface atoms.
The mechanically blended baseline will yield phase separation or elemental clustering.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized by polyol reduction.
The proposed relationship may fail when reduction kinetics, ligand effects, precursor solubility, or coordination chemistry dominate alloying.
Statistically equivalent alloy homogeneity and elemental distribution from both precursor routes would falsify the precursor-uniformity mechanism.
